nodes.title: Foundations and Core Language
nodes.description: This part groups chapters in this subject’s graduate book.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Topological spaces and continuous maps
nodes.description: A topology specifies open sets without requiring a distance function. Continuity is expressed by inverse images of open sets.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Topology axioms
nodes.description: A topology specifies open sets without requiring a distance function. Its axioms retain the set operations needed to discuss continuity and convergence.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Open and closed sets
nodes.description: Open sets belong to the topology, and closed sets are their complements. These classes support neighborhood, closure, and boundary definitions.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Bases and subbases
nodes.description: A basis generates open sets by unions, while a subbasis first allows finite intersections. Both give economical descriptions of a topology.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Generated topologies
nodes.description: A generated topology is the smallest topology containing specified initial sets. This minimality supplies useful comparison and continuity properties.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Continuity
nodes.description: Continuity is expressed by inverse images of open sets. Homeomorphisms identify spaces with exactly the same topological structure.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Preimages
nodes.description: A map is continuous when inverse images of open target sets are open. This definition avoids any reliance on coordinates or metrics.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Homeomorphisms
nodes.description: A homeomorphism is a continuous bijection with continuous inverse. A continuous bijection alone need not be a homeomorphism.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Comparison with metric continuity
nodes.description: For metric spaces, the open-set definition agrees with the usual epsilon-delta condition. This verifies that topology extends familiar analysis.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Subspaces and universal constructions
nodes.description: The subspace topology gives a subset the open sets inherited from its ambient space. Products and disjoint unions assemble spaces with prescribed mapping properties.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Subspaces
nodes.description: The subspace topology gives a subset the open sets inherited from its ambient space. Relative closure and interior must be interpreted in that setting.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Induced topology
nodes.description: The induced topology consists of intersections of ambient open sets with the subset. It makes the inclusion map continuous in a universal way.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Closure and interior
nodes.description: Closure collects points inseparable from a set by neighborhoods, while interior collects contained open neighborhoods. Their values can change when the ambient space changes.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Subspace examples
nodes.description: Intervals and dense subsets illustrate the difference between relative and ambient openness. Such examples prevent incorrect transfer of topological properties.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Products and coproducts
nodes.description: Products and disjoint unions assemble spaces with prescribed mapping properties. The box topology shows that seemingly natural alternatives can behave differently.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Product topology
nodes.description: The product topology is generated by conditions on finitely many coordinates. It is the weakest topology making every projection continuous.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Box topology
nodes.description: The box topology permits independent open restrictions on all coordinates at once. For infinite products it can be strictly finer than the product topology.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Disjoint unions
nodes.description: The disjoint-union topology makes a set open exactly when its intersection with each component is open. It is the categorical coproduct of spaces.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Quotients and identifications
nodes.description: Quotient topology turns identifications into a topological space. Identification spaces create familiar geometric objects and unfamiliar pathologies.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Quotient topology
nodes.description: Quotient topology turns identifications into a topological space. Its defining property controls maps defined on equivalence classes.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Saturated sets
nodes.description: A saturated subset is a union of complete equivalence classes. Such sets are useful for understanding preimages under the quotient map.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Quotient maps
nodes.description: A quotient map is a surjection whose target openness is exactly detected by inverse images. This is stronger than being a continuous surjection.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Universal property
nodes.description: A map out of a quotient is continuous when its composite with the quotient map is continuous. This universal property is the main construction tool.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Applications
nodes.description: Identification spaces create familiar geometric objects and unfamiliar pathologies. The examples expose which separation properties survive the construction.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Identifying boundaries
nodes.description: Gluing boundary points or faces constructs circles, tori, and other spaces. The quotient topology determines how neighborhoods fit across the identifications.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Orbit spaces
nodes.description: An orbit space identifies points related by a group action. Its topology records the geometry remaining after symmetry is removed.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Examples of non-Hausdorff quotients
nodes.description: Quotients can fail to be Hausdorff even when the original space is well behaved. Explicit examples show why closed-orbit or stronger hypotheses may be needed.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Central Theory and Techniques
nodes.description: This part groups chapters in this subject’s graduate book.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Connectedness and compactness
nodes.description: Connectedness excludes decompositions into separated nonempty open pieces. Compactness abstracts the ability to extract finite information from arbitrary open covers.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Connectedness
nodes.description: Connectedness excludes decompositions into separated nonempty open pieces. Local and path versions refine this global property.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Components
nodes.description: Connected components are maximal connected subsets. They partition a space but need not be open.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Local connectedness
nodes.description: Local connectedness means that points have bases of connected neighborhoods. It improves the relation between components and open sets.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Path connectedness
nodes.description: Path connectedness joins each pair of points by a continuous interval map. It implies connectedness, but the converse fails in general.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Compactness
nodes.description: Compactness abstracts the ability to extract finite information from arbitrary open covers. In metric spaces it also has useful sequential characterizations.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Open-cover definition
nodes.description: A compact space has a finite subcover for every open cover. This formulation applies even when sequences do not detect the topology.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Sequential compactness in metric spaces
nodes.description: In metric spaces, compactness is equivalent to every sequence having a convergent subsequence. The equivalence should not be transferred to all topological spaces.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Local compactness
nodes.description: Local compactness gives points compact neighborhoods under the adopted convention. It is important in compactification and function-space theory.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Countability and separation
nodes.description: Countability axioms limit the size of neighborhood and cover data. Separation axioms specify how points and closed sets can be distinguished by neighborhoods.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Countability axioms
nodes.description: Countability axioms limit the size of neighborhood and cover data. They determine when sequences or countable constructions suffice.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: First and second countability
nodes.description: First countability gives countable neighborhood bases at points, while second countability gives one countable basis for the whole space. The latter is stronger.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Separability
nodes.description: Separability means that a countable subset is dense. Its relation to basis countability depends on the category of spaces.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Lindelöf property
nodes.description: A Lindelöf space has a countable subcover for every open cover. This property weakens compactness while retaining useful covering control.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Separation axioms
nodes.description: Separation axioms specify how points and closed sets can be distinguished by neighborhoods. Different theorems require different levels of separation.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: T1 and Hausdorff
nodes.description: T1 means singletons are closed, while Hausdorff means distinct points have disjoint neighborhoods. Hausdorff spaces have unique limits when limits are defined by nets.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Regularity
nodes.description: Regularity separates a point from a disjoint closed set by neighborhoods. The convention concerning an additional T1 requirement should be fixed.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Normality
nodes.description: Normality separates disjoint closed sets by disjoint neighborhoods. It supports continuous separation and extension theorems.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Metrization and completeness
nodes.description: Metrization asks whether a topology arises from some metric. Completeness concerns the existence of limits of Cauchy sequences in a chosen metric.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Metrizable spaces
nodes.description: Metrization asks whether a topology arises from some metric. Countability and separation conditions supply useful sufficient criteria.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Compatible metrics
nodes.description: A compatible metric induces exactly the given topology. Several distinct metrics may be compatible without having the same completeness properties.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Urysohn metrization theorem
nodes.description: Urysohn's metrization theorem gives metrizability for regular second-countable T1 spaces. It converts topological hypotheses into a distance representation.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Examples
nodes.description: Standard manifolds provide metrizable examples under their usual countability assumptions. Nonmetrizable examples show which hypotheses cannot simply be dropped.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Complete metric spaces
nodes.description: Completeness concerns the existence of limits of Cauchy sequences in a chosen metric. Baire category derives strong consequences from this condition.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Completion
nodes.description: Completion embeds a metric space densely into a complete one. It is unique up to the isometry fixing the original space.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Baire category theorem
nodes.description: The Baire category theorem prevents a nonempty complete metric space from being a countable union of nowhere-dense closed sets. Equivalent formulations concern intersections of dense open sets.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Applications
nodes.description: Category arguments prove existence of typical objects and support functional-analysis theorems. Each application must identify a Baire space and the relevant open dense sets.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Compactification and product theorems
nodes.description: Compactification places a space densely inside a compact space. Product compactness is a major theorem whose proof uses covering or convergence methods.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Compactifications
nodes.description: Compactification places a space densely inside a compact space. Different constructions preserve different classes of continuous maps.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: One-point compactification
nodes.description: The one-point compactification adds a point at infinity to a suitable locally compact Hausdorff noncompact space. Its neighborhoods encode complements of compact sets.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Stone–Čech idea
nodes.description: The Stone–Čech compactification of a completely regular Hausdorff space has a universal extension property for maps into compact Hausdorff spaces. It generally adds much more than one point.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Examples
nodes.description: The real line and discrete spaces illustrate different compactification behaviors. Comparing them clarifies how neighborhoods at added points are determined.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Product compactness
nodes.description: Product compactness is a major theorem whose proof uses covering or convergence methods. Its relation to choice reveals a foundational dimension of topology.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Tychonoff theorem
nodes.description: Tychonoff's theorem states that arbitrary products of compact spaces are compact in the product topology. Finite-coordinate neighborhoods are essential to that topology.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Alexander subbase theorem
nodes.description: Alexander's subbase theorem reduces compactness checks to covers from a subbasis under the usual choice setting. It is an efficient route to product compactness.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Choice principles
nodes.description: Some general compactness principles depend on choice principles. Their exact logical strength depends on the class of spaces and the formulation used.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Separation and extension theorems
nodes.description: Urysohn's lemma replaces neighborhood separation with a continuous scalar function. Tietze extends real-valued continuous functions from closed subsets of normal spaces.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Urysohn lemma
nodes.description: Urysohn's lemma replaces neighborhood separation with a continuous scalar function. It is a key consequence of normality.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Normal spaces
nodes.description: Normal spaces separate disjoint closed sets by disjoint open neighborhoods. This is the hypothesis behind the standard continuous-separation construction.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Construction
nodes.description: The construction nests open neighborhoods indexed by dyadic rationals. Taking an infimum produces a continuous function with prescribed endpoint values.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Consequences
nodes.description: Continuous separation supports embeddings, extension theorems, and metrization. It turns qualitative topology into numerical measurements.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Tietze extension
nodes.description: Tietze extends real-valued continuous functions from closed subsets of normal spaces. It strengthens separation into a general extension procedure.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Extension of real-valued functions
nodes.description: Under the standard normal-space hypotheses, a continuous real-valued function on a closed subset extends continuously to the space. Bounded versions preserve a chosen interval range.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Partitions of unity preview
nodes.description: Partitions of unity assemble local data using continuous weights that sum to one. Their existence in useful forms requires additional covering hypotheses such as paracompactness.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Further Theory and Applications
nodes.description: This part groups chapters in this subject’s graduate book.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Function spaces and topological groups
nodes.description: Topologies on function spaces determine what convergence of maps means. A topological group combines algebraic operations with continuity.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Function-space topologies
nodes.description: Topologies on function spaces determine what convergence of maps means. Compact-open and uniform topologies serve different purposes.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Compact-open topology
nodes.description: The compact-open topology controls images of compact subsets inside target open sets. It is a natural topology for continuous mapping spaces.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Uniform convergence
nodes.description: Uniform convergence bounds the pointwise discrepancy over the entire domain using a suitable target structure. It is stronger than convergence on each compact subset in general.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Evaluation maps
nodes.description: Evaluation sends a function and a point to the function value. Its continuity depends on the function-space topology and domain hypotheses.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Topological groups
nodes.description: A topological group combines algebraic operations with continuity. Translation symmetry makes its local and global topology closely related.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Continuity of operations
nodes.description: Multiplication and inversion must be continuous in a topological group. Translations are then homeomorphisms and transport neighborhoods of the identity.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Quotient groups
nodes.description: Quotient groups by normal subgroups inherit a quotient topology. Closedness of the subgroup is important for Hausdorff quotient behavior.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Compact groups
nodes.description: Compact groups combine compact topology with continuous algebraic symmetry. They provide a bridge to Haar measure and representation theory.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Dimension, uniformity, and further topics
nodes.description: Dimension theory measures topological complexity without assuming coordinates. Uniform structures retain a notion of uniformly close pairs without specifying a metric.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Dimension theory
nodes.description: Dimension theory measures topological complexity without assuming coordinates. Its definitions must be distinguished from algebraic or metric notions of dimension.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Covering dimension
nodes.description: Covering dimension bounds the overlap multiplicity needed in refinements of open covers. It is a topological invariant under the appropriate definition.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Examples
nodes.description: Euclidean spaces and totally disconnected compact examples calibrate covering dimension. Carefully chosen examples distinguish it from other dimension notions.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Invariance questions
nodes.description: Dimension invariance asks what constructions or equivalences preserve dimension. Such questions prevent coordinates from being mistaken for intrinsic structure.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Uniform structures
nodes.description: Uniform structures retain a notion of uniformly close pairs without specifying a metric. They extend uniform continuity and completeness beyond metric spaces.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Uniform spaces
nodes.description: A uniform space is described by entourages of the diagonal satisfying compatibility axioms. These encode a uniform notion of closeness.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Completion
nodes.description: Uniform completion adds limits of appropriate Cauchy filters or nets under separation assumptions. It extends metric completion to the uniform setting.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Advanced routes and applications
nodes.description: Uniform spaces connect function spaces, topological groups, and compactification. Further study should specify which additional structures each application uses.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.
